title: What are the window components in detail — window assigner (assigns events to windows), trigger (determines when to fire computation, e.g. EventTimeTrigger, CountTrigger, ProcessingTimeTrigger), and evictor (optionally removes elements before/after window function) — and how do they interact?
shortTitle: What are the window components in Flink

s1_definition.profdef: A Flink window is built from three cooperating components. The window assigner decides, for each incoming element, which window or windows it belongs to, for example a one-minute tumbling window or a set of overlapping sliding windows. The trigger decides when a window's computation should fire and emit a result, based on event-time or processing-time progress or on element counts. The evictor is an optional component that can remove elements from the window's buffer either before or after the window function runs, which lets you keep only a subset such as the most recent elements. The assigner routes, the trigger times, and the evictor prunes.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of the National Bank of India sorting transaction slips into labeled trays. The window assigner is the clerk who reads each slip's time and drops it into the correct minute-labeled tray. The trigger is the supervisor who decides the moment to say "process this tray now and publish its total," which could be "when the clock passes the minute" or "as soon as the tray has one hundred slips." The evictor is an optional helper who, just before or just after the supervisor processes a tray, removes certain slips, for example keeping only the last ten slips so the computation reflects only recent activity. Together they route slips into trays, decide when to add up a tray, and optionally trim what is in it.
s1_definition.oneliner: The assigner puts events into windows, the trigger decides when each window fires, and the optional evictor trims elements around the firing.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A Flink window is built from three cooperating components. The window assigner decides, for each incoming element, which window or windows it belongs to, for example a one-minute tumbling window or a set of overlapping sliding windows. The trigger decides when a window's computation should fire and emit a result, based on event-time or processing-time progress or on element counts. The evictor is an optional component that can remove elements from the window's buffer either before or after the window function runs, which lets you keep only a subset such as the most recent elements. The assigner routes, the trigger times, and the evictor prunes.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of the National Bank of India sorting transaction slips into labeled trays. The window assigner is the clerk who reads each slip's time and drops it into the correct minute-labeled tray. The trigger is the supervisor who decides the moment to say "process this tray now and publish its total," which could be "when the clock passes the minute" or "as soon as the tray has one hundred slips." The evictor is an optional helper who, just before or just after the supervisor processes a tray, removes certain slips, for example keeping only the last ten slips so the computation reflects only recent activity. Together they route slips into trays, decide when to add up a tray, and optionally trim what is in it.

**One line to remember:** The assigner puts events into windows, the trigger decides when each window fires, and the optional evictor trims elements around the firing.

sections.s2_technical:
The window assigner is set by the window call. `TumblingEventTimeWindows.of(Time.minutes(1))` assigns each element to exactly one non-overlapping minute window based on its event time. `SlidingEventTimeWindows.of(Time.minutes(1), Time.seconds(10))` assigns each element to multiple overlapping windows. `EventTimeSessionWindows.withGap(Time.minutes(5))` assigns elements into windows that merge as long as the gap between them is under five minutes. `GlobalWindows.create()` assigns every element to a single global window. Each assigner also declares a default trigger that matches its semantics.

The trigger decides when the window function actually runs. Every window assigner comes with a sensible default trigger: event-time windows default to `EventTimeTrigger`, which fires when the watermark passes the window end; processing-time windows default to `ProcessingTimeTrigger`, which fires on the wall clock; and the global window has no useful default, so you must supply one such as `CountTrigger.of(100)`, which fires every hundred elements. A trigger's callbacks return a `TriggerResult` that can be CONTINUE (do nothing), FIRE (run the function and emit but keep the window contents), PURGE (clear the window), or FIRE_AND_PURGE (emit then clear). You can override the default with `.trigger(...)` to build custom firing logic, for example a trigger that fires early every ten seconds and then finally on the watermark, giving speculative results plus a final correct one.

The evictor is optional and is attached with `.evictor(...)`. It runs around the window function, and its two callbacks, `evictBefore` and `evictAfter`, can remove elements from the window buffer. `CountEvictor.of(10)` keeps only the last ten elements, `TimeEvictor.of(Time.seconds(30))` keeps only elements within the last thirty seconds of the largest timestamp, and `DeltaEvictor` removes elements that differ from the last element by more than a threshold. The important senior nuance is that using an evictor forces Flink to buffer every element in the window rather than incrementally aggregate, because it must have the raw elements available to evict them, which disables the memory-efficient incremental aggregation path and can use far more memory. So you only use an evictor when you genuinely need element-level pruning, and otherwise prefer a plain reduce or aggregate. The three components interact in a strict order: for each element the assigner selects its windows and adds it to each window's buffer, the trigger is consulted and may say fire, and if an evictor is present it prunes the buffer before and after the window function runs on the surviving elements.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India wants a per-account average transaction amount computed over one-minute windows, but it only wants the average of the ten most recent transactions in each minute, because very old transactions within the minute are less relevant for its live risk score. The plain window would average all transactions in the minute, so we need something that trims the buffer to the last ten before computing. This is exactly the role of a count evictor working together with the assigner and trigger.

Problem 2 — The risk team also wants a speculative early result emitted partway through the minute, not only at the end, so they can react sooner, while still getting a final corrected result when the minute closes. This is exactly the role of a custom trigger that fires early and then fires again at the window end, layered on top of the same assigner.

In the mini-project we build a runnable demo reproducing the assigner, trigger, and evictor interaction. We define a `RiskTxn` with an event time and amount. A `WindowAssigner` floors each transaction into its one-minute window. A `CountTriggerPolicy` reproduces a trigger that fires early every N elements and finally at the window end. A `LastNEvictor` keeps only the most recent ten elements of a window before the average is computed. A `WindowComponentsEngine` wires the three together: for each element it assigns the window, buffers the element, asks the trigger whether to fire, and if firing, applies the evictor then computes the average. A `WindowComponentsDemo` main class feeds twelve Rajesh transactions into one minute, shows an early speculative firing, shows the evictor dropping the two oldest so only the last ten count, and shows the final firing at window end.

```yaml
# application.yml
flink:
  components:
    window-seconds: 60
    trigger-every-n: 5     # early speculative fire every 5 elements
    evictor-keep-last: 10  # keep only the last 10 elements
```

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: twelve transactions for Rajesh (SAV2001) with amounts 100, 200, up to 1200, all stamped within the 10:00 window (event times 0 to 11 seconds). The trigger fires every five elements, and the evictor keeps only the last ten.

Step 1: The assigner floors every transaction's event time to the 10:00 window start, so all twelve belong to one window. Each transaction is added to the window buffer as it arrives.

Step 2: After the fifth transaction, the count trigger returns fire, so a speculative result is emitted. The buffer has five elements, which is fewer than the evictor's keep-last-ten, so the evictor keeps all five and the average of 100 through 500 is computed as 300.

Step 3: After the tenth transaction, the trigger fires again. The buffer has ten elements, still equal to keep-last-ten, so all ten survive and the average of 100 through 1000 is 550.

Step 4: The eleventh and twelfth transactions arrive, growing the buffer to twelve, but the trigger only fires on multiples of five, so no speculative fire happens at eleven or twelve.

Step 5: The window end is reached and the engine performs the final fire. Now the buffer has twelve elements but the evictor keeps only the last ten, so it drops the two oldest, 100 and 200, and computes the average of 300 through 1200, which is 750. This is the final corrected result the risk team records.

Step 6: After the final fire the buffer is purged, freeing memory, and the window is done. The demo has shown all three components cooperating: the assigner grouped everything into one window, the trigger produced two speculative results plus one final result, and the evictor trimmed the buffer to the last ten before each computation.

Final output:

```
2026-10-30 07:41:00 [INFO] SPECULATIVE FIRE window=0 avg(last 5 of 5) = 300.00
2026-10-30 07:41:00 [INFO] SPECULATIVE FIRE window=0 avg(last 10 of 10) = 550.00
2026-10-30 07:41:00 [INFO] FINAL FIRE window=0 avg(last 10 of 12) = 750.00
```

```
  12 RiskTxn (amounts 100..1200, all in 10:00 window)
    │
    ▼
  WindowAssigner  (floor eventTime to 60s window)
    │ all 12 → window [0,60s)
    ▼
  WindowComponentsEngine buffer: [100,200,...,1200]
    │
    ├─ CountTriggerPolicy.onElement(count % 5 == 0) ──→ FIRE?

    │ speculative@5  = 300.00
    │ speculative@10 = 550.00
    │ FINAL@end      = 750.00  (last 10 of 12)
    ▼

```

```
  7.   → buffer.clear()  (PURGE)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
A Flink window is not a single thing; it is built from three cooperating components, and understanding how they interact is what separates surface knowledge from real understanding. The window assigner decides, for every incoming element, which window or windows it belongs to. A tumbling assigner puts an element into exactly one non-overlapping window, a sliding assigner can put one element into several overlapping windows, a session assigner groups bursts separated by gaps, and the global assigner puts everything into a single window. The trigger decides when a window actually fires and emits a result. Event-time windows default to a trigger that fires when the watermark passes the window end, processing-time windows fire on the wall clock, and count-based firing happens every N elements. A trigger returns a result that can continue, fire, purge, or fire and purge, and you can supply a custom trigger to emit speculative early results and then a final correct one. The evictor is optional and runs around the window function; it can remove elements from the buffer before or after the computation, for example keeping only the most recent N elements or only those within a recent time span.

The interaction has a strict order. For each element, the assigner selects its windows and the element is buffered into each one. The trigger is then consulted and may say fire. If a window fires and an evictor is present, the evictor prunes the buffer before the window function runs and may prune again afterward, and the function computes over the survivors. A crucial senior-level point is that attaching an evictor forces Flink to retain every raw element in the window instead of aggregating incrementally, because it must have the elements available to evict them, so it disables the memory-efficient incremental path and can use much more memory. For that reason you only reach for an evictor when you truly need element-level pruning.

At the National Bank of India I used this composition for a live per-account risk average. The assigner was a one-minute tumbling event-time window, I attached a custom trigger that fired speculatively every few transactions so the risk dashboard updated quickly, and I used a count evictor that kept only the ten most recent transactions so the average reflected current behavior rather than the whole minute. I could demonstrate the three working together: all transactions assigned to the same minute, speculative results emitted partway through, and a final result at the minute's end where the evictor dropped the oldest transactions before computing. I was also careful to justify the evictor, because it meant buffering raw transactions and giving up incremental aggregation, and that memory cost is exactly the kind of tradeoff a principal engineer is expected to call out.
